A common path is: study commerce or marketing → join a retail or wholesale company as a purchasing assistant → learn product selection and supplier management → independently manage a category → advance to purchasing manager.

This career suits people with a feel for both markets and people, who are comfortable with numbers and can handle inventory pressure. If you are willing to study data and visit markets repeatedly to build a season's assortment, this could be the right field for you.

paragraphs: At the start of the month, review last season's sell-through and margins and flag bestsellers and excess inventory. Travel to trade shows to select new products and negotiate prices and payment terms with suppliers. Back at the office, use forecasting systems to calculate purchase quantities and avoid overstocking. After launch, monitor conversion daily, promote and clear slow sellers quickly, and keep bestsellers in stock.

In a sentence: they decide what goes on the shelves. Their work includes analyzing and selecting products, sourcing suppliers and negotiating prices, setting purchase quantities and controlling inventory, monitoring margins and clearing slow sellers, scouting new products at trade shows, and coordinating launches with marketing. The goal is to pick winners, prevent stockouts, and minimize excess inventory.

paragraphs: A 7/10 means this occupation sits in a moderately high-exposure area of commerce data: forecasting, replenishment, and monitoring can all be accelerated, but product selection and negotiation remain human responsibilities.

But moderately high exposure does not mean high risk: AI replaces the calculating and replenishing, not the selecting and negotiating. Buyers with strong market instincts who can pick winning products will become scarcer. The vulnerable role is the data clerk who only handles replenishment.

This career suits people who combine market instinct, financial discipline, and accountability—those who can make the right product bets using both data and intuition, and withstand inventory pressure.

What this career develops most is instinct: one winning product can save an entire season, while a bad bet can leave piles of excess inventory. It suits people with a feel for markets and people who are also comfortable with numbers.
Prefers business decision-making while also being practical and rule-oriented (Enterprising E + Conventional C + Social S).
If you enjoy the sense of control that comes from picking one product that saves an entire season—and you are willing to visit markets and work through the numbers—this career can be addictive.
